title: Separating a gas mixture without changing its particles
subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
stem: The sealed vessel contains the particles shown. Filled atoms are X and open atoms are Y. A selective membrane passes only X₂ particles; it does not split any particle. Every drawn particle represents the same number of real particles. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the elemental substances and compound, and calculate the X: Y atom ratio in the original vessel.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: All X₂ passes through the membrane. Find the fraction of original particles remaining and the fraction of remaining particles that are XY₂.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why this process is a physical separation and why it cannot produce a sample containing only separate X atoms.

steps.text: X₂ and Y₂ are elements; XY₂ is a compound.
Count 2 X₂, 3 Y₂ and 4 XY₂: X atoms = 8, Y atoms = 14.
There were 9 particles and 7 remain.
Remaining fraction 7/9; XY₂ fraction among those remaining 4/7.
No bonds within X₂, Y₂ or XY₂ have been broken or formed.
The membrane selects intact particles by a physical property.
Obtaining separate X atoms from these substances would require breaking covalent bonds, which this process does not do.

title: Interpreting two plateaus on a heating curve
subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
stem: A pure substance is heated at constant power. The schematic curve has melting plateau B–C lasting 4.0 min at 0.0 °C and boiling plateau D–E lasting 12.0 min at 100.0 °C. No energy is lost. For a fixed sample, supplied energy equals power × time. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the phases present on each plateau and explain why temperature remains constant although energy is supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Compare the energy supplied during vaporization with that during melting.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare the average kinetic energies at the two plateaus. Explain why 100/0 is not a valid calculation.

steps.text: B–C: solid and liquid; D–E: liquid and gas.
Energy changes intermolecular separation/arrangement rather than increasing mean particle kinetic energy.
Temperature, which measures average kinetic energy on the kelvin scale, therefore remains constant during each phase change.
Constant power makes energy proportional to plateau duration.
Vaporization energy is 12.0/4.0 = 3.0 times melting energy.
Use absolute temperatures 273.15 K and 373.15 K.
Ratio = 373.15/273.15 = 1.37 to 3 significant figures.
Celsius zero is not zero kinetic energy; only absolute temperature has the required proportionality.

title: An isotope collection and its charged particles
stem: The drawing is a counted collection of ten silicon atoms, not a mass spectrum: eight have 14 neutrons, one has 15, and one has 16. Every atom has atomic number 14. Treat isotope masses as their integer mass numbers. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the three isotope symbols and find the mean relative atomic mass of this collection.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: One atom of the heaviest isotope forms Si²⁺. State its proton, neutron and electron counts and explain which counts change.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A second ten-atom collection has the same total number of protons but a larger mass. Explain whether it must have the same isotope abundances and whether its ordinary chemical behavior should be very different.

steps.text: Use the counted abundances 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1.
Mean relative atomic mass = 28.3, without units.
14 protons, 16 neutrons and 12 electrons.
Only two electrons are lost; the nucleus and isotope identity are unchanged.
Same total proton count for ten Si atoms does not fix neutron count or isotope abundances.
A larger mass can result from a greater proportion of heavier isotopes.
Neutral isotopes have the same electron configuration, so their ordinary chemistry is very similar; physical isotope effects can occur.

title: Repairing three proposed orbital diagrams
stem: The diagrams are a student’s proposed condensed configurations. The neutral atoms have Z(Cr)=24 and Z(Cu)=29; Fe has Z=26. The Fe²⁺ row shows only electrons outside [Ar]. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Correct the neutral Cr and Cu configurations, explaining the specific errors.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Correct the Fe²⁺ configuration and draw its five 3d orbital boxes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a box containing two upward arrows is invalid, and count the unpaired electrons in ground-state Cr and Fe²⁺.

steps.text: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.
The proposed 4s²3d⁴ and 4s²3d⁹ arrangements ignore the ground-state exceptions.
The corrected d counts correspond to half-filled d⁵ and filled d¹⁰ sublevels; retain the total electron counts.
Neutral Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s²; remove the two 4s electrons first.
Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶: one paired 3d box and four singly occupied boxes with parallel unpaired spins.
Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins: Pauli exclusion principle.
Cr has 6 unpaired electrons, including 4s¹; Fe²⁺ has 4.
Hund’s rule places electrons singly in degenerate d orbitals before pairing.

title: Combustion traps reveal an oxygen-containing formula
subtopic: Counting particles by mass: The mole
stem: A 0.900 g compound contains only C, H and O. Complete combustion produces 1.320 g CO₂ and 0.540 g H₂O. Its independently measured molar mass is 90.0 g mol⁻¹. Use C=12.0, H=1.0 and O=16.0. The traps separately collect all CO₂ and all H₂O. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the amounts of C and H atoms in the sample and the mass of O originally present.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the empirical and molecular formulas.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why counting every O atom in the CO₂ and H₂O as originally belonging to the sample would be incorrect.

steps.text: Masses C=0.360 g and H=0.0600 g.
Empirical formula CH₂O; empirical formula mass 30.0.
90.0/30.0=3, so molecular formula C₃H₆O₃.

stem: For equal amounts of gases A and B at the same temperature, the graph shows measured pV against pressure. The horizontal reference is the ideal value nRT. steps.text: Particles have negligible volume, and intermolecular attractions are negligible.

Find ideal minimum energies, assuming one threshold photon per ionization. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare and calculate the first ionization energies.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the absorbed energy needed to ionize0.0150 mol of ground-state X atoms.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the minimum supplied lamp energy and explain why a real experiment may require more.

steps.text: Shorter convergence wavelength means higher photon energy.
IE=hcNₐ/(1000λ), with λ in metres.
X: 798 and Y: 399 kJ mol⁻¹; X is exactly twiceY under the given data.
Multiply molar IE by the amount, not by an additional Avogadro factor.
Absorbed minimum=12 kJ.
Supplied energy=absorbed energy/0.250.
Minimum supplied=47.9 kJ.
The calculation assumes threshold-energy photons and one successful ionization for every photon in the stated useful fraction; other losses or unsuccessful interactions increase the demand.

title: A convergence limit from an excited level is not the first IE
stem: Two hydrogen series converge at 91.2 nm and 364.8 nm. Their lower levels are n=1 and n=2 respectively. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Set the energy of a free electron plus H⁺ to zero. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the limit giving first ionization energy and calculate it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the molar energies of levels n=1 and n=2 relative to zero and the energy of emission2→1.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the wavelength of that line and explain the fourfold relation between the two ionization thresholds.

steps.text: First IE removes the electron from ground level n=1, so use91.2 nm.
IE=hcNₐ/(1000λ).
First IE=1.31e+03 kJ mol⁻¹.
Emitted energy=E₂−E₁, a positive quantity.
Photon energy for 2→1=985 kJ mol⁻¹.
Use hc/λ₂₁ = hc/91.2 nm − hc/364.8 nm.
λ₂₁=121.6 nm.
Ionization from n=2 needs one quarter of the ground-state energy because its convergence wavelength is four times as long; this does not make it the first IE.

stem: A ground-state atomic emission series obeys the supplied relation f=K(1−1/n²), where n labels an excited bound level. The graph of f against1/n² is linear. The line passes through(0.25, 2.475×10¹⁵ Hz) and(0.0400, 3.168×10¹⁵ Hz). Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find first ionization energy and convergence wavelength.

parts.label: c

steps.text: Gradient=−3.30×10¹⁵ Hz.
The intercept at 1/n²=0 is K=3.30×10¹⁵ Hz.
IE=hKNₐ/1000 andλ=c/K.
IE=1.32×10³ kJ mol⁻¹; λ=90.9 nm to 3 significant figures.
As n increases, 1/n² approaches zero, so f approachesK.
Every finite n has1/n²>0 and f<K.
The levels converge toward the ionization limit; each finite line is a transition from a bound state, not from the free-electron limit.

title: Selective photoionization in a one-photon regime
stem: Ground-state ionization thresholds correspond to 250 nm for X atoms and 180 nm for Y atoms. A mixture is exposed to 200 nm photons. Each absorption involves one atom and one photon; simultaneous multiple-photon processes are excluded. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify which element can be ionized and explain the wavelength comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the200 nm photon energy and the molar thresholds for X and Y.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the energy per mole of 200 nm photons above X’s threshold and explain why merely increasing the intensity of 600 nm light cannot cross that threshold under these assumptions.

steps.text: A photon must have wavelength no longer than the threshold to supply sufficient energy.
200 nm can ionizeX, but cannot ionizeY.
Its energy exceeds the250 nm threshold but is below the180 nm threshold.
Use E=hc/λ and multiply threshold photon energies by Nₐ/1000.
200 nm photon energy=9.945×10⁻¹⁹ J.
X threshold=479; Y threshold=665 kJ mol⁻¹.
Subtract the X threshold from the molar 200 nm photon energy.
Excess=120 kJ per mole of photons.
Greater intensity supplies more600 nm photons, but each remains below the required single-photon energy; the excluded multiple-photon process cannot be assumed.

title: A bright visible line cannot replace a convergence limit
stem: A neutral gaseous atom has a bright emission line at 650 nm. Its series ending at the ground level converges at 80.0 nm. A student uses the bright line to report first ionization energy. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: b

title: A spectrum measured from cations determines a second IE
stem: A series recorded from gaseous Mg⁺ ions terminates at the ground level of Mg⁺ and converges at 3.63544×10¹⁵ Hz. Neutral Mg has first IE 738 kJ mol⁻¹. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴, c=3.00×10⁸, Nₐ=6.02×10²³ in SI units. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the ionization represented by this limit and explain why its energy is not Mg’s first IE.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy represented by the limit and the total energy per mole for Mg(g)→Mg²⁺(g)+2e⁻.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the energy for 0.0400 mol of initially neutral Mg to become Mg²⁺ and compare the Mg⁺ and neutral Mg electron configurations.

steps.text: Mg⁺(g) → Mg²⁺(g)+e⁻.
The starting species is a singly charged ion, so the limit measures removal of its next electron.
It is the second IE relative to neutral Mg’s successive-ionization sequence.
IE₂=hfNₐ/1000≈1451 kJ mol⁻¹.
Total=738+1451≈2189 kJ mol⁻¹.
Use 0.0400 times the sum of both ionization energies.
87.6 kJ to 3 significant figures.
Mg: [Ne]3s²; Mg⁺: [Ne]3s¹. Both removed electrons originate in 3s, but the second is held more strongly by the positive ion.

steps.text: The marked jump is after the fifth removed electron.
Five valence electrons imply group 15; the period 3 element is phosphorus.
Its ground configuration is[Ne]3s²3p³; removal6 begins from the lower[Ne]core.

First five sum17070 kJ mol⁻¹; sixth alone21267 kJ mol⁻¹.
A single core electron therefore costs more to remove than all five valence electrons combined.

Sample energy 383 kJ to 3 significant figures.
Equal log-axis separations represent equal ratios, not equal additive IE differences.
